transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks wrong. My nose and jaw seem crooked, especially in ID pictures or on the online class camera. People tell me they don’t see it, but I feel like everyone in the CNC lab notices my face before they notice anything I do.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your reflection in mirrors or cameras throughout the day?

Yeah. Before school I can get stuck checking the bathroom mirror and my phone camera over and over. I’ll fix my hair, change shirts trying to hide the angle of my face, and ask my mom if it looks weird. Sometimes it takes so long I miss lab, or I get there too exhausted to focus.
Deep down, do you feel there is any possibility that your face might actually look normal and your mind is exaggerating it, or are you completely convinced of the flaw?

I mean, people keep telling me it looks normal, but I don’t really believe them. When I see pictures or the camera, it just looks obviously crooked to me. It feels like people at the lab have to notice it.
Aside from your concerns about your face, do you have any other repetitive thoughts or rituals, such as excessive cleaning, checking locks, or needing things in a particular order?
No, not really. It’s mostly the stuff with my face. I don’t think I have other rituals like that.
Do you believe that people around you are actively talking about or mocking your face?

I don’t know if they’re actually talking about it, but I feel like they notice it right away. In the CNC lab, I’m thinking they see how crooked the left side of my face looks before they even pay attention to my work.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance (facial asymmetry) that is not noticeable to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors (frequent mirror/camera checking, camouflaging, reassurance-seeking) and significant functional impairment (missing school labs, concentration difficulties). In ICD-10, body dysmorphic disorder is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder).

confirmed_symptoms: Preoccupation with perceived physical defect in appearance (left side of face, nose, and jaw appearing crooked)
Repetitive mirror and phone camera checking
Camouflaging behavior (adjusting hair and clothing to hide face)
Ideas of reference regarding perceived physical flaw

additional_requirements: Absence of general obsessive-compulsive rituals (cleaning, checking locks, ordering denied)
Non-delusional insight (acknowledges others state it looks normal, though difficult to believe)
